issues.legal_issue: A tenant who receives only part of the leased premises may be required to pay rent proportionate to the premises received rather than being entitled to suspend all rent.
material_facts: The lease covered a flat with three bedrooms, but the landlord delivered possession of only two bedrooms.
The tenant withheld all rent despite possessing and using a substantial part of the premises without much inconvenience.
issues.conclusion: The tenant was not entitled to suspend all rent and was liable to pay proportionate rent for the premises received.
issues.legal_principle: Applying Ram Lal Dutt Sarkar v. Dhirendra Nath Roy, [1943] 70 I.A. 18, the Court held that the doctrine of suspension of rent is not an inflexible rule and its application depends on the circumstances of each case. It would be inequitable to let a tenant use a substantial part of the leased property without compensation, just as it would be inequitable to demand full rent when the whole premises had not been delivered. The Court declined to apply the inflexible approach associated with Neale v. Mackenzie, 150 E.R. 635, in every case.

rule.if: rent_arrears_recovery_suit and landlord_delivered_only_part and tenant_withheld_all_rent and tenant_used_substantial_part_without_much_inconvenience

predicates.rent_arrears_recovery_suit: A landlord brought a suit to recover unpaid rent from a tenant.
predicates.landlord_delivered_only_part: The landlord gave the tenant possession of only part of the premises covered by the lease.
predicates.tenant_withheld_all_rent: The tenant stopped paying all rent despite receiving possession of part of the premises.
predicates.tenant_used_substantial_part_without_muc: The tenant used a substantial portion of the leased premises without much inconvenience.

issues.definition: When a tenant withholds all rent in a rent-recovery suit despite using a substantial part of the premises delivered without much inconvenience, the tenant must pay rent proportionate to the premises received.

issues.legal_issue: A court should not refuse to consider apportionment of rent solely because the tenant did not specifically plead that relief in the written statement when the circumstances call for determining the proportionate rent.
material_facts: The landlord had not delivered the whole of the leased premises.
The tenant had raised proportionate rent as an alternative to dismissal of the rent claim during the proceedings in the High Court.
The High Court rejected apportionment on technical grounds, including the absence of a specific plea in the written statement and a request to amend it.
The tenant and landlord could lead evidence on apportionment, but the lower courts had not determined the proportionate rent.
issues.conclusion: The orders below were set aside and the suit was remanded for determination of proportionate rent, with the parties at liberty to lead evidence on that issue.
issues.legal_principle: It is inequitable to allow a landlord to recover full rent when the landlord did not deliver possession of the whole premises. In the circumstances, a technical objection based on the absence of a specific plea should not prevent consideration of apportionment; the matter should be remanded so the proportionate rent can be determined on evidence.

predicates.rent_arrears_recovery_suit: A landlord brought a suit to recover unpaid rent from a tenant.
predicates.landlord_delivered_only_part: The landlord gave the tenant possession of only part of the premises covered by the lease.
predicates.tenant_asserted_proportionate_rent_as_al: The tenant asked for rent to be apportioned as an alternative to rejecting the landlord's claim altogether.
predicates.lower_courts_rejected_apportionment_on_t: The lower courts declined to determine proportionate rent because of a technical objection concerning the tenant's pleading.

issues.definition: When a tenant seeks proportionate rent as an alternative in a rent-recovery suit, and the lower courts reject apportionment on technical pleading grounds despite partial delivery of the premises, the suit must be remanded to determine proportionate rent.

issues.legal_issue: A court exercising supervisory jurisdiction may consider the merits of a rent dispute and correct an erroneous decision even though supervisory jurisdiction is ordinarily used sparingly.
material_facts: The tenant challenged the rent decisions in an application invoking the revisional jurisdiction under the Code of Civil Procedure and the supervisory jurisdiction under the Constitution.
The High Court considered the merits rather than dismissing the application solely because of limits on its revisional jurisdiction.
The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was right not to reject the application on that ground, given the circumstances.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was right not to dismiss the application solely on the ground that supervisory jurisdiction should ordinarily be used sparingly.
issues.legal_principle: The Court recognized that supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution should ordinarily be used sparingly. It nevertheless held that the application, which also invoked section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, should not be rejected without consideration on that ground in the circumstances of this case.

predicates.rent_dispute_challenged_in_revision_and_: A party challenged a decision in a rent dispute through proceedings invoking both revisional and supervisory jurisdiction.
predicates.challenged_decision_requires_correction: The challenged decision contains an error that calls for correction.

issues.definition: When a rent-dispute decision is challenged through revision and supervisory proceedings and requires correction, the supervisory court may consider the merits.
